slides.text: After the car crash shattered my ankle and ended my career with the Royal Ballet, I moved to a quiet lane in Kyoto where nobody knew my name. Every afternoon, I watched Kenji through the window of his tiny ceramic studio. With a squirrel-hair brush and urushi lacquer dusted in twenty-four-karat gold, he mended broken teabowls, turning their jagged cracks into rivers of light.

One rainy Tuesday, I limped inside carrying a porcelain swan I had smashed in a fit of grief. 'Can you hide the break?' I asked, keeping my scarred ankle tucked behind my long skirt. Kenji turned the shards gently in his calloused palms and shook his head. 'In kintsugi, Clara, we never disguise the fracture. To pretend a vessel was never broken is to rob it of the history it survived.'

For six months, he taught me to mix gold dust into resin while I taught him English idioms over steaming genmaicha. On the evening we finished my porcelain swan, he knelt beside my stool, gently rolled up the hem of my skirt, and pressed his warm thumb along the silver surgical scar on my ankle. 'You see a ruin,' he whispered, looking up at me with reverence. 'I have never seen anything hold the light like you.'
